danish.title: Første bog (1805) — Kapitel 17
paragraphs: Efter at Anna Mikhajlovna var kørt af sted med sin søn til grev Kirill Vladimirovitj Bezukhov, sad grevinde Rostova længe helt alene og pressede lommetørklædet mod øjnene. Til sidst ringede hun.
»Hvad er der i vejen, min kære?« sagde hun irriteret til pigen, der lod hende vente et par minutter. »Ønsker du ikke at betjene mig? Så finder jeg en anden plads til dig.«

Grevinden var oprørt over sin venindes sorg og ydmygende fattigdom og var derfor i dårligt humør — en sindstilstand, der hos hende altid gav sig udslag i, at hun kaldte pigen 'min kære' og talte til hende med overdreven høflighed.
»Jeg beklager meget, frue,« svarede pigen.
»Bed greven komme ind til mig.«
Greven kom vuggende ind til sin hustru med sit sædvanlige lidt skyldige udtryk.
»Nå, lille grevinde! Sikken en sauté af vildt au madère vi får, min kære! Jeg smagte på den. De tusind rubler, jeg gav for Taras, var ikke spildt. Han er dem værd!«
Han satte sig ved sin kones side, armene på knæene og hænderne rodende i det grå hår.
»Hvad befaler min lille grevinde?«
»Jo, ser du, min kære... Hvad er det for noget svineri?« sagde hun og pegede på hans vest. »Det er nok sautéen,« tilføjede hun med et smil. »Jo, ser du, greve, jeg har brug for penge.«
Hendes ansigt blev bedrøvet.
»Åh, lille grevinde!« ... og greven begyndte travlt at lede efter sin tegnebog.
»Jeg har brug for mange penge, greve! Jeg har brug for fem hundrede rubler,« og hun tog sit batisttørklæde frem og begyndte at tørre sin mands vest.
»Straks, straks! Hej, er der nogen?« råbte han i en tone, som kun bruges af folk, der er sikre på, at de, de kalder på, vil styrte til. »Send Dmitrij ind til mig!«
Dmitrij, en mand af god familie, der var vokset op i grevens hus og nu bestyrede alle hans anliggender, trådte blødt ind i stuen.

»Her er sagen, min kære ven,« sagde greven til den ærbødige unge mand, der var kommet ind. »Hent mig...« han tænkte sig om et øjeblik, »ja, hent mig syv hundrede rubler. Men husk, bring mig ikke sådanne pjaltede og snavsede sedler som sidst — pæne, rene til grevinden.«
»Ja, Dmitrij, rene sedler, om jeg må be,« sagde grevinden med et dybt suk.

»Hvornår ønsker Deres Excellence dem?« spurgte Dmitrij. »Tillad mig at oplyse... Men bliv ikke urolig,« tilføjede han hurtigt, da han bemærkede, at greven begyndte at trække vejret tungt og hurtigt — altid et tegn på forestående vrede. »Jeg var lige ved at glemme... Ønsker De dem bragt med det samme?«
»Ja, ja; netop! Bring dem. Giv dem til grevinden.«
»Sikke en skat, den Dmitrij er,« tilføjede greven med et smil, da den unge mand var gået. »Der findes aldrig noget 'umuligt' med ham. Dét er noget, jeg afskyr! Alt er muligt.«
»Åh, penge, greve, penge! Hvor megen sorg de volder i verden,« sagde grevinden. »Men jeg har hårdt brug for den sum.«
»Du, min lille grevinde, er en notorisk ødeland,« sagde greven og kyssede sin kones hånd, før han gik tilbage til sit kontor.
Da Anna Mikhajlovna vendte tilbage fra grev Bezukhov, lå pengene — lutter rene sedler — klar under et lommetørklæde på grevindens lille bord, og Anna Mikhajlovna bemærkede, at noget bekymrede hende.
»Nå, min kære?« spurgte grevinden.
»Åh, i hvilken forfærdelig tilstand han er! Man ville ikke genkende ham, så syg er han! Jeg var der kun et øjeblik og sagde næsten ikke et ord...«
»Annette, for himlens skyld, afslå det ikke,« begyndte grevinden med en rødmen, der så besynderlig ud på hendes tynde, værdige, aldrende ansigt, og hun tog pengene frem under lommetørklædet.
Anna Mikhajlovna fornam øjeblikkeligt hendes hensigt og bøjede sig, parat til at omfavne grevinden i det rette øjeblik.
»Dette er til Boris fra mig — til hans udrustning.«

Anna Mikhajlovna omfavnede hende allerede og græd. Grevinden græd også. De græd, fordi de var veninder, og fordi de var gode mennesker, og fordi de — veninder siden barndommen — var nødt til at tænke på noget så lavt som penge, og fordi deres ungdom var forbi... Men de tårer var behagelige for dem begge.

english.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: After Anna Mikhaylovna had driven off with her son to visit Count Cyril Vladimirovich Bezukhov, Countess Rostova sat alone for a long time, pressing her handkerchief to her eyes. At last she rang the bell.
"What's the matter with you, my dear?" she said irritably to the maid who had kept her waiting several minutes. "Don't you want to serve me? Then I'll find you another position."

The countess was upset by her friend's sorrow and humiliating poverty, and was therefore in a bad mood—a state that, with her, always expressed itself in calling her maid "my dear" and speaking to her with exaggerated politeness.
"I'm very sorry, ma'am," the maid replied.
"Ask the count to come to me."
The count came waddling in to see his wife, looking somewhat guilty as usual.
"Well, little countess! What a game stew in Madeira sauce we're going to have, my dear! I tried it. The thousand rubles I paid for Taras were well spent. He's worth it!"
He sat down beside his wife, elbows on his knees, running his hands through his gray hair.
"What are your orders, little countess?"
"You see, my dear... What's that mess?" she said, pointing at his waistcoat. "It's the stew, most likely," she added with a smile. "Well, the thing is, Count, I need some money."
Her face turned sad.
"Oh, little countess!"... And the count began fumbling for his pocketbook.
"I need a lot, Count! I need five hundred rubles," and taking out her cambric handkerchief, she began wiping her husband's waistcoat.
"Yes, right away, right away! Hey, who's there?" he called out in a tone used only by people who are certain their summons will be instantly obeyed. "Send Dmitri to me!"
Dmitri, a man from a good family who had been raised in the count's household and now managed all his affairs, stepped quietly into the room.

"This is what I need, my dear fellow," said the count to the respectful young man. "Bring me..." He thought for a moment. "Yes, bring me seven hundred rubles. But make sure you don't bring me tattered, dirty notes like last time—nice clean ones, for the countess."
"Yes, Dmitri, clean ones, please," said the countess with a deep sigh.

"When would you like them, your excellency?" asked Dmitri. "If I may mention... But don't worry," he added quickly, noticing that the count was beginning to breathe hard and fast—always a sign that anger was approaching. "I forgot... Shall I bring them right away?"
"Yes, yes, just so! Bring it. Give it to the countess."
"What a treasure that Dmitri is," the count added with a smile when the young man had gone. "There's never any 'impossible' with him. That's a thing I can't stand! Everything is possible."
"Ah, money, Count, money! What sorrow it causes in this world," said the countess. "But I desperately need this sum."
"You, my little countess, are a well-known spendthrift," said the count, and having kissed his wife's hand, he went back to his study.

When Anna Mikhaylovna returned from Count Bezukhov's, the money—all in clean notes—was lying ready under a handkerchief on the countess's little table. Anna Mikhaylovna could see that something was troubling her friend.
"Well, my dear?" asked the countess.
"Oh, what a terrible state he's in! You wouldn't recognize him, he's so ill! I was only there a few minutes and barely said a word..."
"Annette, for heaven's sake, don't refuse me," the countess began, with a blush that looked very strange on her thin, dignified, elderly face, and she took the money from under the handkerchief.
Anna Mikhaylovna instantly guessed what she intended and bent forward, ready to embrace the countess at the right moment.
"This is for Boris, from me—for his outfit."

Anna Mikhaylovna was already embracing her and weeping. The countess wept too. They wept because they were friends, and because they were kind-hearted, and because they—friends since childhood—had to think about such a base thing as money, and because their youth was over. But those tears were pleasant to them both.
